Object-state changes during language processing

Debriefing Form
column4:
> What are we trying to learn in this research?
The goal of this research is to understand how different features of concepts are activated during sentence processing, and whether attention to these features changes as the object is modified during the reading of the sentence.

Why is this important to scientists or the general public?
This experiment has both theoretical and practical implications. Theoretically, it will help scientists better understand the ways in which humans represent events and the objects within those events and prioritize different features of objects during sentence processing. Practically, it will help us understand how to build better event-centric models of language that would benefit AI-centric settings.

Where can I learn more?
Horchak, O. V., & Garrido, M. V. (2020). Dropping bowling balls on tomatoes: Representations of object state-changes during sentence processing. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition.

What if I have questions?
If you have any questions about the research study, please contact Abhilasha Kumar at: a.kumar@bowdoin.edu

Thank you for participating!

column2: > Your task is to decide how ""squashable"" different objects are by rating them as:

column1: **Important** : ""Squashable"" refers to how likely it is that a given object would shatter, fall apart, crack, splatter, etc. if a heavy object (such as a bowling ball) were dropped on it. In other words, would you expect the object to become permanently deformed, dismembered, etc. in such a way that it is considered broken, squashed, smashed, etc. after dropping a heavy object onto it? A squashable object is in some way ""breakable"" and permanently deforms with heavy force.
It is important that you make your judgements as quickly as possible , without significantly overthinking your answer. If you do not know what the object is, make your best guess (do not Google it).
The survey should take <strong> no more than 4 minutes <strong> (there are 32 objects).

Object-state changes during language processing

Debriefing Form
column4:
> What are we trying to learn in this research?
The goal of this research is to understand how different features of concepts are activated during sentence processing, and whether attention to these features changes as the object is modified during the reading of the sentence.

Why is this important to scientists or the general public?
This experiment has both theoretical and practical implications. Theoretically, it will help scientists better understand the ways in which humans represent events and the objects within those events and prioritize different features of objects during sentence processing. Practically, it will help us understand how to build better event-centric models of language that would benefit AI-centric settings.

Where can I learn more?
Horchak, O. V., & Garrido, M. V. (2020). Dropping bowling balls on tomatoes: Representations of object state-changes during sentence processing. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition.

What if I have questions?
If you have any questions about the research study, please contact Abhilasha Kumar at: a.kumar@bowdoin.edu

Thank you for participating!

column2: > Your task is to decide how ""squashable"" different objects are by rating them as:

column1: **Important** : ""Squashable"" refers to how likely it is that a given object would shatter, fall apart, crack, splatter, etc. if a heavy object (such as a bowling ball) were dropped on it. In other words, would you expect the object to become permanently deformed, dismembered, etc. in such a way that it is considered broken, squashed, smashed, etc. after dropping a heavy object onto it? A squashable object is in some way ""breakable"" and permanently deforms with heavy force.
It is important that you make your judgements as quickly as possible , without significantly overthinking your answer. If you do not know what the object is, make your best guess (do not Google it).
The survey should take <strong> no more than 4 minutes <strong> (there are 32 objects).

Object-state changes during language processing

Debriefing Form
column4:
> What are we trying to learn in this research?
The goal of this research is to understand how different features of concepts are activated during sentence processing, and whether attention to these features changes as the object is modified during the reading of the sentence.

Why is this important to scientists or the general public?
This experiment has both theoretical and practical implications. Theoretically, it will help scientists better understand the ways in which humans represent events and the objects within those events and prioritize different features of objects during sentence processing. Practically, it will help us understand how to build better event-centric models of language that would benefit AI-centric settings.

Where can I learn more?
Horchak, O. V., & Garrido, M. V. (2020). Dropping bowling balls on tomatoes: Representations of object state-changes during sentence processing. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition.

What if I have questions?
If you have any questions about the research study, please contact Abhilasha Kumar at: a.kumar@bowdoin.edu

Thank you for participating!

column2: > Your task is to decide how ""squashable"" different objects are by rating them as:

column1: **Important** : ""Squashable"" refers to how likely it is that a given object would shatter, fall apart, crack, splatter, etc. if a heavy object (such as a bowling ball) were dropped on it. In other words, would you expect the object to become permanently deformed, dismembered, etc. in such a way that it is considered broken, squashed, smashed, etc. after dropping a heavy object onto it? A squashable object is in some way ""breakable"" and permanently deforms with heavy force.
It is important that you make your judgements as quickly as possible , without significantly overthinking your answer. If you do not know what the object is, make your best guess (do not Google it).
The survey should take <strong> no more than 4 minutes <strong> (there are 32 objects).

Object-state changes during language processing

Debriefing Form
column4:
> What are we trying to learn in this research?
The goal of this research is to understand how different features of concepts are activated during sentence processing, and whether attention to these features changes as the object is modified during the reading of the sentence.

Why is this important to scientists or the general public?
This experiment has both theoretical and practical implications. Theoretically, it will help scientists better understand the ways in which humans represent events and the objects within those events and prioritize different features of objects during sentence processing. Practically, it will help us understand how to build better event-centric models of language that would benefit AI-centric settings.

Where can I learn more?
Horchak, O. V., & Garrido, M. V. (2020). Dropping bowling balls on tomatoes: Representations of object state-changes during sentence processing. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition.

What if I have questions?
If you have any questions about the research study, please contact Abhilasha Kumar at: a.kumar@bowdoin.edu

Thank you for participating!

Object-state changes during language processing

Debriefing Form
column3:
> What are we trying to learn in this research?
The goal of this research is to understand how different features of concepts are activated during sentence processing, and whether attention to these features changes as the object is modified during the reading of the sentence.

Why is this important to scientists or the general public?
This experiment has both theoretical and practical implications. Theoretically, it will help scientists better understand the ways in which humans represent events and the objects within those events and prioritize different features of objects during sentence processing. Practically, it will help us understand how to build better event-centric models of language that would benefit AI-centric settings.

Where can I learn more?
Horchak, O. V., & Garrido, M. V. (2020). Dropping bowling balls on tomatoes: Representations of object state-changes during sentence processing. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition.

What if I have questions?
If you have any questions about the research study, please contact Abhilasha Kumar at: a.kumar@bowdoin.edu

Thank you for participating!

column2: > Your task is to decide how ""squashable"" different objects are by rating them as:

column1: **Important** : ""Squashable"" refers to how likely it is that a given object would shatter, fall apart, crack, splatter, etc. if a heavy object (such as a bowling ball) were dropped on it. In other words, would you expect the object to become permanently deformed, dismembered, etc. in such a way that it is considered broken, squashed, smashed, etc. after dropping a heavy object onto it? A squashable object is in some way ""breakable"" and permanently deforms with heavy force.
It is important that you make your judgements as quickly as possible , without significantly overthinking your answer. If you do not know what the object is, make your best guess (do not Google it).
The survey should take <strong> no more than 4 minutes <strong> (there are 32 objects).

Object-state changes during language processing

Debriefing Form
column4:
> What are we trying to learn in this research?
The goal of this research is to understand how different features of concepts are activated during sentence processing, and whether attention to these features changes as the object is modified during the reading of the sentence.

Why is this important to scientists or the general public?
This experiment has both theoretical and practical implications. Theoretically, it will help scientists better understand the ways in which humans represent events and the objects within those events and prioritize different features of objects during sentence processing. Practically, it will help us understand how to build better event-centric models of language that would benefit AI-centric settings.

Where can I learn more?
Horchak, O. V., & Garrido, M. V. (2020). Dropping bowling balls on tomatoes: Representations of object state-changes during sentence processing. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition.

What if I have questions?
If you have any questions about the research study, please contact Abhilasha Kumar at: a.kumar@bowdoin.edu

Thank you for participating!

column2: > Your task is to decide how ""squashable"" different objects are by rating them as:

column1: **Important** : ""Squashable"" refers to how likely it is that a given object would shatter, fall apart, crack, splatter, etc. if a heavy object (such as a bowling ball) were dropped on it. In other words, would you expect the object to become permanently deformed, dismembered, etc. in such a way that it is considered broken, squashed, smashed, etc. after dropping a heavy object onto it? A squashable object is in some way ""breakable"" and permanently deforms with heavy force.
It is important that you make your judgements as quickly as possible , without significantly overthinking your answer. If you do not know what the object is, make your best guess (do not Google it).
The survey should take <strong> no more than 4 minutes <strong> (there are 32 objects).

Object-state changes during language processing

Debriefing Form
column4:
> What are we trying to learn in this research?
The goal of this research is to understand how different features of concepts are activated during sentence processing, and whether attention to these features changes as the object is modified during the reading of the sentence.

Why is this important to scientists or the general public?
This experiment has both theoretical and practical implications. Theoretically, it will help scientists better understand the ways in which humans represent events and the objects within those events and prioritize different features of objects during sentence processing. Practically, it will help us understand how to build better event-centric models of language that would benefit AI-centric settings.

Where can I learn more?
Horchak, O. V., & Garrido, M. V. (2020). Dropping bowling balls on tomatoes: Representations of object state-changes during sentence processing. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition.

What if I have questions?
If you have any questions about the research study, please contact Abhilasha Kumar at: a.kumar@bowdoin.edu

Thank you for participating!

column2: > Your task is to decide how ""squashable"" different objects are by rating them as:

column1: **Important** : ""Squashable"" refers to how likely it is that a given object would shatter, fall apart, crack, splatter, etc. if a heavy object (such as a bowling ball) were dropped on it. In other words, would you expect the object to become permanently deformed, dismembered, etc. in such a way that it is considered broken, squashed, smashed, etc. after dropping a heavy object onto it? A squashable object is in some way ""breakable"" and permanently deforms with heavy force.
It is important that you make your judgements as quickly as possible , without significantly overthinking your answer. If you do not know what the object is, make your best guess (do not Google it).
The survey should take <strong> no more than 4 minutes <strong> (there are 32 objects).

Object-state changes during language processing

Debriefing Form
column4:
> What are we trying to learn in this research?
The goal of this research is to understand how different features of concepts are activated during sentence processing, and whether attention to these features changes as the object is modified during the reading of the sentence.

Why is this important to scientists or the general public?
This experiment has both theoretical and practical implications. Theoretically, it will help scientists better understand the ways in which humans represent events and the objects within those events and prioritize different features of objects during sentence processing. Practically, it will help us understand how to build better event-centric models of language that would benefit AI-centric settings.

Where can I learn more?
Horchak, O. V., & Garrido, M. V. (2020). Dropping bowling balls on tomatoes: Representations of object state-changes during sentence processing. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition.

What if I have questions?
If you have any questions about the research study, please contact Abhilasha Kumar at: a.kumar@bowdoin.edu

Thank you for participating!

It is important that you make your judgements as quickly as possible , without significantly overthinking your answer. If you do not know what the object is, make your best guess (do not Google it).

Object-state changes during language processing

Debriefing Form
column3:
> What are we trying to learn in this research?
The goal of this research is to understand how different features of concepts are activated during sentence processing, and whether attention to these features changes as the object is modified during the reading of the sentence.

Why is this important to scientists or the general public?
This experiment has both theoretical and practical implications. Theoretically, it will help scientists better understand the ways in which humans represent events and the objects within those events and prioritize different features of objects during sentence processing. Practically, it will help us understand how to build better event-centric models of language that would benefit AI-centric settings.

Where can I learn more?
Horchak, O. V., & Garrido, M. V. (2020). Dropping bowling balls on tomatoes: Representations of object state-changes during sentence processing. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition.

What if I have questions?
If you have any questions about the research study, please contact Abhilasha Kumar at: a.kumar@bowdoin.edu

Thank you for participating!

column2: > Your task is to decide how ""squashable"" different objects are by rating them as:

column1: **Important** : ""Squashable"" refers to how likely it is that a given object would shatter, fall apart, crack, splatter, etc. if a heavy object (such as a bowling ball) were dropped on it. In other words, would you expect the object to become permanently deformed, dismembered, etc. in such a way that it is considered broken, squashed, smashed, etc. after dropping a heavy object onto it? A squashable object is in some way ""breakable"" and permanently deforms with heavy force.
It is important that you make your judgements as quickly as possible , without significantly overthinking your answer. If you do not know what the object is, make your best guess (do not Google it).
The survey should take <strong> no more than 4 minutes <strong> (there are 32 objects).

Object-state changes during language processing

Debriefing Form
column4:
> What are we trying to learn in this research?
The goal of this research is to understand how different features of concepts are activated during sentence processing, and whether attention to these features changes as the object is modified during the reading of the sentence.

Why is this important to scientists or the general public?
This experiment has both theoretical and practical implications. Theoretically, it will help scientists better understand the ways in which humans represent events and the objects within those events and prioritize different features of objects during sentence processing. Practically, it will help us understand how to build better event-centric models of language that would benefit AI-centric settings.

Where can I learn more?
Horchak, O. V., & Garrido, M. V. (2020). Dropping bowling balls on tomatoes: Representations of object state-changes during sentence processing. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition.

What if I have questions?
If you have any questions about the research study, please contact Abhilasha Kumar at: a.kumar@bowdoin.edu

Thank you for participating!
